values.title: Six weeks.
values.text: One skill a week, in the order you need them at work: say it plainly first, then handle what goes wrong, then make it sound like you. Each week ends with something you can put in a portfolio.

values.title: What you learn, and what you hand in
values.intro: Open a week to see what it covers and its exercise. Every exercise uses a real screen, a brief and a word limit.

steps.title: Week 1: Say it plainly
steps.text:
Plain language, front-loading and sentence length. You learn to cut a screen to half its words without losing meaning.
Exercise: rewrite the first three screens of a banking app’s onboarding in 120 words.

steps.title: Week 2: When things go wrong
steps.text:
Error messages, empty states and confirmations. Every message answers three questions: what happened, why, and what to do next.
Exercise: rewrite five errors from a checkout flow.
steps.linkLabel: Read a sample lesson from this week

steps.title: Week 3: Buttons, labels and forms
steps.text:
Verbs on buttons, labels versus placeholders, help text and the order of fields.
Exercise: redo a nine-field sign-up form and justify every label in one line.

steps.title: Week 4: Voice and tone
steps.text:
What a product voice is, how tone bends with the situation, and how to write it down so other people can use it.
Exercise: a one-page voice chart for a product you know.

steps.title: Week 5: Everyone can read it
steps.text:
Writing for screen readers, alt text, reading levels and text that survives translation into longer languages.
Exercise: audit one flow and fix its ten worst lines.

steps.title: Week 6: Prove it and ship it
steps.text:
Cloze tests, five-second tests and how to present a change so it gets approved.
Capstone: a before and after case study of one flow, presented to your group.

values.title: One password reset email, annotated

items.note: Week 1. The subject line is the action. No “Important notice”, no exclamation mark.

items.text: Someone asked to reset the password for hannah@example.com. If that was you, choose a new one with the button below. The link works for 30 minutes.
items.note: Week 2. Say what happened, then what to do, then the limit. In that order.
Week 3. A button finishes the sentence “I want to”. “Click here” and “Submit” never do.

items.text: If you didn’t ask for this, you can ignore this email. Your password stays the same and nobody has seen it.
items.note: Week 4. Calm, not chirpy. The reader may be worried, so the tone drops a notch.

values.title: Six words you will use with confidence
values.intro: You will hear these in every workshop. By week three you will be the one explaining them in meetings.

items.definition: The small words inside a product: labels, buttons, hints, errors and confirmations.
items.example: “The microcopy on that form is doing the work of a help page.”

items.definition: To put the most useful words first, because most people read only the start of a line.
The personality of a product’s writing. It stays the same on every screen.
items.example: “Our voice is a calm colleague, not a mascot.”

items.definition: How the voice adapts to the moment: lighter after a success, plainer after an error.
items.example: “Nobody wants a joke when a payment fails.”

items.definition: What a screen says before there is anything to show, and the best place to explain what to do next.
items.example: “The empty state should be the tutorial.”

items.definition: A test where readers fill in every fifth word you removed. Above 60% right means the text is clear.
items.example: “The new terms page scored 71% on a cloze test.”

values.status: Teaching the winter cohort from January 11
values.title: Hi, I’m Ines Okafor. I teach people to write the words inside products
values.text: For fifteen years I wrote the buttons, errors and emails for banking and travel apps. Since 2021 I have taught 1,900 designers, developers and product managers to do the same, from my desk in Lisbon.

values.title: Fifteen years of small words
values.body:
Ines started as a support agent at a travel company, answering the questions its website failed to answer. She moved to the product team to fix them at the source, and has written for interfaces ever since.

She led content design at Kestrel Pay for six years, where her team cut payment support tickets by a third by rewriting 140 error messages. She started Plainspoken in 2021 because every course she could find taught marketing copy, not interface text.

values.title: “Nobody reads, so every word has to earn its place”
values.intro: Tomas Reyes took the course in 2022 and now runs the Plainspoken community. He asked Ines the questions new students ask him.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Most people think of writing as a talent. Can you really teach it in six weeks?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Interface writing is closer to a craft than a talent. There are about twenty rules, and you can learn to apply them the way you learn to use a grid. What takes six weeks is the habit of applying them every time.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Who struggles most in the course?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: People who write well. They are attached to their sentences. The developers and the people writing in a second language often do best, because they are happy to cut.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why is everything built around feedback?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Because you can’t see your own unclear sentence. You know what you meant. A stranger reading it cold in a feedback group finds the problem in ten seconds.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What do you want a graduate to do on the Monday after?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Open their own product, find the worst error message and fix it before lunch. Then show someone the before and after. That is how the work spreads.

values.title: To whoever is nervous about showing their writing to strangers
values.body:
Every cohort, someone writes to me in week one to say they nearly didn’t post their first draft. It felt too rough, or their English wasn’t good enough, or everyone else seemed to be a real writer.

Here is what I tell them. Nobody in your group is a real writer. They are designers and developers and product managers who got handed the words, same as you. And a rough draft is the only kind we can do anything with.

The feedback is specific and kind. We talk about the sentence, never the person. By week three you will be the one spotting what is wrong with mine.
values.name: Ines Okafor

values.title: Read the opening of a week two lesson
values.issueTitle: The error message is the product
values.excerpt:
When a payment fails, nobody admires your layout. They read one sentence, and that sentence decides whether they try again or leave.

Most error messages are written last, by whoever is closest to the code, in the five minutes before release. That is why they sound like the code: “Invalid input”, “Request failed”, “Error 4012”.

A good error answers three questions in order. What happened? Why? What can I do now? Take the card error from this week’s exercise and try it yourself before you read on.

values.title: Everything else, sorted by topic
values.intro: Jump to a topic or read the lot. We update this page after every cohort with the questions we were asked most.

questions.question: Who is the course for?
questions.answer: Designers, developers, product managers and support leads who write the words in a product without having trained as writers. Working writers who are new to interfaces take it too.

questions.question: What will I be able to do at the end?
questions.answer: Rewrite any screen so a first-time reader understands it, explain your choices with rules instead of taste, and test whether the new text is clearer. You also leave with four portfolio pieces.

questions.question: How is the cohort different from self-paced?
questions.answer: The lessons are identical. In the cohort you also get six live workshops, written feedback on every exercise and a feedback group of six people. Self-paced students get model answers instead.

questions.question: How much time does it take?
questions.answer: Three to four hours a week: about one hour of lessons, one to two hours on the exercise and 75 minutes for the workshop.

questions.question: What if I can’t make Thursdays?
questions.answer: Every workshop is recorded, captioned and posted within the hour. About 4 in 10 students watch the recording. You can send your draft in advance and still have it discussed.

questions.question: What if I fall behind?
questions.answer: You have until two weeks after the last workshop to hand in exercises and still get feedback. If life gets in the way entirely, you can move to the next cohort once, at no cost.

questions.question: Can I pay in instalments?
questions.answer: Yes. The Cohort plan can be paid in three monthly payments of $240, and Cohort plus coaching in three of $410. There is no credit check.

questions.question: How does the refund work?
questions.answer: Write to hello@plainspoken.example within 14 days of the cohort starting and we refund the full amount within five working days. Self-paced students have 14 days from the day they buy.

questions.question: Will my employer pay?
questions.answer: Often, yes. We send an invoice with your company’s details and a one-page summary of the course you can forward to your manager. About half of our students are funded this way.

questions.question: How long do I keep access?
questions.answer: For as long as the course exists. That includes every lesson, the recordings from your own cohort and any lessons we add later.

questions.question: Is the certificate worth anything?
questions.answer: It shows you handed in the work, which is what hiring managers ask us about. The portfolio pieces matter more, and we tell you so.

questions.question: Is there a community afterwards?
questions.answer: Yes. Graduates keep their feedback group channel and get a monthly open workshop where Ines rewrites screens that members send in.
